title: Assessment of rodent-borne disease (Lassa Fever) and its health implications in Kpakiama Community, Bomadi
abstract: Lassa fever is a zoonotic viral disease of public health importance in West Africa, with transmission associated with human exposure to infected rodent reservoirs and contaminated environments. This study assessed perceived risk factors, knowledge, and health implications of Lassa fever among adult residents of Kpakiama Community, Bomadi Local Government Area, Delta State, Nigeria. Specifically, the study examined perceived factors associated with Lassa fever transmission, perceived public health implications, perceived economic impacts, and measures for prevention and control. A descriptive cross-sectional survey design was adopted. A sample of 150 adult residents was selected from the six quarters of the community using stratified and simple random sampling techniques. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analysed using frequencies and percentages. The findings showed substantial agreement among respondents that environmental, infrastructural, knowledge-related, cultural, and behavioural factors may contribute to Lassa fever transmission. Respondents also reported perceived public health and economic consequences associated with Lassa fever and identified early reporting, community sanitation, and other preventive practices as important measures for prevention and control. Because the study was based on self-reported questionnaire data and did not involve laboratory confirmation of Lassa virus infection, the findings should be interpreted as evidence of community perceptions, reported practices, and perceived health implications rather than as confirmation of active Lassa fever transmission in Kpakiama. The study recommends strengthened community health education, improved environmental sanitation and waste management, safe food storage, early reporting of suspected cases, and improved access to appropriate healthcare services.

title: Lassa Fever Prevention, Surveillance and Outbreak Response in West Africa: Scoping Review of Policies, Implementation, Barriers and Gaps
abstract: Lassa fever is an acute viral illness caused by Lassa virus, a zoonotic pathogen maintained in rodents and transmitted to humans through contact with infected animals or their excreta and, secondarily, from person to person. The disease is endemic in parts of West Africa, with Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Liberia, and Guinea carrying the greatest recognised burden, with estimates of severity varying with setting and case ascertainment. No vaccine or antiviral is licensed or approved for Lassa fever. Control, therefore, rests almost entirely on public health measures: reducing contact between rodents and people, infection prevention and control, early detection and notification, laboratory confirmation, contact tracing, risk communication, and coordinated emergency response. Existing syntheses thus address either Lassa fever epidemiology, clinical outcomes, transmission modelling, environmental drivers, and vaccine candidates or outbreak response across several pathogens at once. Notably absent is a synthesis that takes Lassa fever policy as its object and asks what is prescribed, what is implemented, at which level of the health system, and why gaps persist. A scoping review is the appropriate design for this question. The aim is to map the extent, range, and nature of a heterogeneous body of evidence, comprising policy documents, after-action reviews, outbreak reports, and qualitative and quantitative studies, and to identify gaps, and not to estimate the effectiveness of a defined intervention. The objective of this review, therefore, is to map the published and grey literature on Lassa fever prevention, surveillance, and outbreak response policies in West Africa; the extent to which they have been implemented; and the barriers, facilitators, and gaps reported at regional, national, subnational, health facility, and community levels.

The disease is endemic in parts of West Africa, with Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Liberia, and Guinea carrying the greatest recognised burden, with estimates of severity varying with setting and case ascertainment. title: Data from In Vitro Inhibition of STAT5 Signaling Limits CD8+ T-cell Exhaustion and Improves Outcomes in Adoptive T-cell Therapy
abstract: Abstract T-cell exhaustion remains a barrier to adoptive cell therapies. Although γc cytokines are used to expand T cells, their impact on T-cell states remains incompletely defined. Using an in vitro model of repetitive T-cell receptor stimulation, we found that high-dose interleukin 2 (IL2) or IL15 promoted exhausted CD8+ T-cell (TEX) differentiation, with increased inhibitory receptor expression and loss of stem-like features. During chronic lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus clone 13 infection, high IL2Rβ expression marked virus-specific CD8+ T cells with features of terminally exhausted T cells, whereas IL2Rβ deficiency favored progenitor-like populations. In TEX, IL2 and IL15 preferentially induced STAT5 phosphorylation over other signaling pathways. Genetic disruption of STAT5 similarly supported progenitor subsets, implicating STAT5 in the progression toward more differentiated TEX states under chronic stimulation. We therefore asked whether transient STAT5 attenuation during in vitro T-cell expansion could bias differentiation toward progenitor-like populations without compromising functional competence. Transient JAK3 or STAT5 inhibition enriched TCF1+Ly108+ progenitor–like cells while preserving cytokine production and degranulation capacity. Following transfer into tumor-bearing mice, cells expanded under STAT5-inhibited conditions mediated superior tumor control and prolonged survival. Likewise, transient STAT5 inhibition preserved memory–progenitor phenotypes in human CD22 chimeric antigen receptor T cells without impairing cytotoxicity. RNA sequencing of STAT5 inhibitor–expanded CD8+ T cells confirmed reinforced stem-like transcriptional programs and reduced enrichment of effector and exhausted signatures. Together, these findings identify the IL2Rβ–STAT5 axis as a regulator of CD8+ T-cell differentiation and support transient STAT5 modulation during ex vivo expansion to improve therapeutic T-cell products.

full_text: Nature Reviews Microbiology nature reviews microbiology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41579-026-01372-1 Review article Check for updates Towards broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals against RNA viruses Hendrik Jan Thibaut 1, Dirk Jochmans 1,3, Christophe Van Dijck2,3, Manon Laporte 1,3, Laurens Liesenborghs 2 & Johan Neyts1 Abstract Small molecule antiviral drugs have transformed the management of infections such as those caused by HIV, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, herpesviruses and influenza viruses. Effective antiviral therapeutics remain unavailable for many other often life-threatening viral infections, many of which are caused by RNA viruses. The development of potent, safe and orally available antivirals is therefore essential both to address current unmet medical needs and to strengthen epidemic and pandemic preparedness. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for building a diversified portfolio of broader-spectrum antivirals against RNA viruses with activity spanning multiple genera, entire families or even crossing viral families. We provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved and investigational antiviral agents active against RNA viruses and discuss the biological determinants that underlie their antiviral spectrum. Finally, we outline the clinical development frameworks required to accelerate the evaluation of such drugs, in particular in the context of outbreaks. Antiviral drug development has so far largely been focused on viral infections that offer large and predict- able commercial markets (for example, those caused by HIV and HCV). It is obviously unrealistic and economically unsustainable to develop specific antiviral drugs for each known viral pathogen. Newly emerging viruses will most likely belong to viral families already known (Table 1) today. Advances in metagenomics and high-throughput sequencing greatly expanded our understanding of viral diversity, and although new viral families may still be discovered, such events are becoming increasingly rare. Together, this strongly supports a strategy in which broader-acting small molecule antiviral (BSA) drugs are developed. Such drugs can be used for the treatment and prophylaxis of infec- tions with known viruses for which no antiviral treatment is available and, in the case of epidemics or pandemics, as a rapid response option while other countermeasures, such as vaccines and mAbs, are being developed12,13. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for the development of BSAs and provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved or experi- mental antiviral drugs active against viruses with an RNA genome. We also outline strategies for target discovery and accelerated clinical development. One drug to treat them all? The term ‘broad-spectrum’ antiviral has been widely used but lacks, to the best of our knowledge, a clear definition. Here, we propose instead to use the term ‘broader-spectrum’ antivirals and distinguish three categories: (i) cross-family BSAs with activity across unrelated viral families within or across a certain genome architecture, that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA); (ii) pan-family BSAs that act across the different genera of a given viral family (for example, pan-paramyxovirus drugs); and (iii) intra-family BSAs, which are active against multiple serotypes and genotypes of a particular virus (for example, pan-serotype dengue virus (DENV) Introduction Viruses, whether known or yet to emerge (‘virus X’), remain a major threat to global health. Vaccines, monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and antiviral drugs are each important and complementary in controlling viral infections. Vaccination has led to the eradication of smallpox, brought polio close to eradication and massively reduced disease and mortality associated with numerous viral infections, such as measles virus, mumps virus, rubella virus, influenza virus, severe acute respira- tory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), hepatitis B virus (HBV) and human papillomavirus1–3. For several important human pathogens, such as HIV, hepatitis C virus (HCV), herpes simplex viruses (HSV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), rhinoviruses and many others, the devel- opment of highly effective vaccines has proved difficult or remains elusive, often despite decades of intensive effort. Therefore, it cannot be guaranteed that efficacious vaccines can always be developed when new threatening viruses emerge4,5. mAbs can offer immediate protection and are transforming the prophylaxis or treatment of certain acute viral diseases, such as those caused by the rabies virus6 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)7. They generally have an excellent safety profile and can be highly effective, although they require injections, are virus specific or variant spe- cific and can rapidly select for escape variants8,9. Like vaccines, mAbs can be developed only once a new pathogen has been identified and characterized. By contrast, small molecule antiviral drugs offer several distinct advantages. They can be administered orally and have the potential to cover a broader spectrum of viruses (Box 1) than vaccines and mAbs. Antiviral drugs have revolutionized the treatment of certain (chronic) viral infections such as those caused by either HIV, HBV, HCV, HSV-1 and HSV-2, and CMV. More recently, antiviral drugs have also become availa- ble against some other viruses including influenza viruses, SARS-CoV-2 and hepatitis delta virus. However, for the majority of the more than 200 known human pathogenic viruses, no antiviral drugs are available. Most of these viruses are RNA viruses — the focus of this Review — including many emerging and clinically important pathogens10–12. Box 1 | Categories and examples of broader-spectrum antivirals (BSAs) for RNA viruses Cross-family BSAs Active against viruses belonging to different (related or unrelated) viral families or across a certain genome architecture (that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA viruses)), typically by targeting conserved features of the viral replication machinery such as the catalytic site of viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerases. For example, remdesivir, a nucleoside viral polymerase inhibitor, is active against viruses belonging to different viral families, that is, the (−)ssRNA Filoviridae, Paramyxoviridae, Pneumoviridae and Arenaviridae as well as the (+) ssRNA Flaviviridae, Picornaviridae and Coronaviridae. Baloxavir, an endonuclease inhibitor, inhibits influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae) but also, although much less potently, several members of the family Peribunyaviridae. Pan-family BSAs Active across all or at least most genera within a single viral family. Examples include neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir, zanamivir and peramivir that are active against both influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae). Nirmatrelvir is a reversible covalent, peptidomimetic Mpro inhibitor that inhibits human and animal coronaviruses belonging to different genera within the family Coronaviridae. Intra-family BSAs Can be active against multiple serotypes, genotypes or strains of a particular virus species. For example, mosnodenvir is active against all dengue virus genotypes (family Flaviviridae) by blocking the interaction between viral proteins NS4B and NS3. Intra-family broader-spectrum activity may span several viruses within one genus of a particular family without extending to other genera. For example, the non-covalent, non-peptidomimetic Mpro inhibitor ensitrelvir is active only against members of the genus Betacoronavirus (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), SARS-CoV-1 and human coronavirus (HCoV)-OC43), but not against members of the genus Alphacoronavirus (such as HCoV-229E and HCoV-NL63) within the family Coronaviridae. Nature Reviews Microbiology Review article inhibitors) or active against one or more (but not all) genera of a viral family (Box 1). The need for broader-acting antivirals and their desired spectrum of activity are mostly defined by the particular (clinical) context (Boxes 2 and 3). For viruses that cause a high number of annual cases (for example, RSV), there might be a sufficiently large market, and thus incentives, to develop virus-specific drugs. Conversely, there might be no or less financial incentive to develop virus-specific drugs for viruses that cause a rather limited number of cases but that col- lectively, within their genus or family, are responsible for a substan- tial clinical burden (for example, coxsackieviruses and echoviruses, EV-D68 and EV-A71 that all belong to the genus Enterovirus). In this case, the development of antivirals that are broadly active across the entire Enterovirus genus (pan-Enterovirus; category intra-family BSAs) represents a more realistic approach. In the context of epidemic or pan- demic preparedness, access to pan-family and cross-family BSAs may be particularly important, as it cannot be predicted which viral family a newly emerging pathogen (‘virus X’) will belong to. Given the extensive genetic diversity and distinct replication strategies of viral families, the development of a single cross-family drug with potent activity against all RNA virus families is likely to be unrealistic. Rather, a more feasible strategy may be to establish a portfolio of different types of BSAs that collectively provide, either alone or in combination, coverage across the RNA virus landscape. BSAs may also be valuable in the context of viral co-infections, in which a single drug could simultaneously target two (or more) viruses14,15. Beyond the spectrum of activity, BSA development must be guided by clearly defined target product profiles16. To have a meaningful clinical impact, BSAs (or combinations thereof) should ideally be highly efficacious, be orally available (preferably once daily dosing), be safe for a broad patient population (preferably including pregnant women and children), possess a (relatively) high barrier to resistance and exhibit minimal drug–drug interactions16. Virus tissue tropism further influences desirable drug properties. For example, infections involving the central nervous system require efficient blood–brain barrier penetration, whereas limited penetration may be preferable for peripheral viral infections. Consequently, distinct target product profiles may be required, even within a single viral genus. The importance of preparedness against known viruses (such as EV-D6818, Ebola virus19, monkeypox virus20 and Andes hantavirus21) as well as against emerging viral threats (for example, SARS-CoV-2) has been repeatedly illustrated during outbreaks caused by these diverse viral pathogens. During the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19 pan- demic), no antiviral drugs were available at the onset. A stockpile of an oral, pan-family coronavirus BSA before the start of the COVID-19 pan- demic would likely have saved countless lives22,23. Remdesivir, originally discovered as an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) inhibitor of RSV24 and Ebola viruses25,26, was the only drug for which antiviral activity against coronaviruses had been systematically demonstrated in preclinical models before the pandemic27. In the absence of readily available and effective antiviral treat- ments, drug repurposing may need to be considered. Repurpos- ing can provide a rapid and relatively cost-effective response by leveraging de-risked drugs with existing preclinical and clinical safety data28,29. However, drugs developed or used for non-viral indi- cations are mostly unlikely to possess sufficient antiviral potency to curb outbreaks caused by newly emerging and (potentially highly) pathogenic viruses. At the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, extensive repurposing initiatives studied whether drugs approved for other indications could inhibit SARS-CoV-2 replication. Drugs such as azithro- mycin (antibiotic), itraconazole (antifungal), hydroxychloroquine (antimalarial, antirheumatic), niclosamide (anthelmintic), ivermectin (anthelmintic) and nitazoxanide (antiparasitic) rapidly entered numer- ous clinical trials, many of them small and underpowered, and even became, for some time, standard treatment in certain settings despite limited preclinical evidence30. Overall, drug repurposing efforts dur- ing the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic were largely unsuccessful, highlighting that such strategies should not be initiated only at the time a new virus emerges. A more realistic approach is to systematically assess existing drugs during epidemic or pandemic ‘peace-time’ against panels of viruses that are representative of high-risk families. Drugs with ‘reason- able’ in vitro activity can be further tested, alone or in combinations, in preclinical models13. Studies in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters revealed that combi- nations of two or three antivirals, each used at suboptimal or even inactive doses, can result in important antiviral effects31. To ration- ally develop combination strategies for BSAs, systematic preclinical testing of combinations across viral families is required. Extensive preclinical studies of the most promising combinations may help to guide strategies for stockpiling for epidemic or pandemic prepared- ness. The use of fixed-dose combinations (such as those used in the treatment of HIV infections) would be ideal. Yet, in outbreak situation with new pathogens, there will be insufficient time to develop such fixed-dose combinations; co-administration of individual drugs would therefore represent a more practical approach. Newly emerging viruses will most likely belong to viral families already known (Table 1) today. Advances in metagenomics and high-throughput sequencing greatly expanded our understanding of viral diversity, and although new viral families may still be discovered, such events are becoming increasingly rare. Together, this strongly supports a strategy in which broader-acting small molecule antiviral (BSA) drugs are developed. The review also outlines the clinical development frameworks required to accelerate the evaluation of such drugs, especially in outbreak scenarios. The authors call for sustained investment in antiviral research to expand therapeutic options.
